0. The big picture in one paragraph

The task is tracking: not just "where are the cells" but "which cell at time t is the same cell at time t+1". So the unit that is scored is not a point — it is an edge, a directed link between a cell at t and its future self at t+1. The metric works in three stages: (1) match predicted cell centres to GT cell centres by distance; (2) using those matches, decide which predicted edges are correct → an edge Jaccard, then multiply by a penalty for detecting the wrong number of cells; (3) separately score whether each GT division (a cell splitting into two) was recovered → a division Jaccard. The two are combined with a 10:1 weight.

1. Stage 1 — Node matching (the 7 µm bipartite gate)

Before any edge can be judged, each predicted cell centre must be paired with a GT cell centre. The matcher (DistanceMatching) builds a bipartite assignment: a predicted node may match a GT node only if their physical distance (using the anisotropic voxel scale (1.625, 0.406, 0.406) µm) is ≤ 7 µm, and each GT node is used at most once.

Why 7 µm? From the dataset statistics, cells move a median of only ~1.8 µm between frames (p95 ≈ 5.3 µm). A 7 µm gate is generous enough to catch a moved cell but tight enough that you can't match a cell to its neighbour. Because coordinates are matched in microns, if you trained on down-sampled data you MUST convert predicted coordinates back to full resolution — a 1-voxel error at down-sample 1,4,4 is ~1.6 µm, which eats into the budget.

2. Stage 2 — Edge Jaccard (the main term)

An edge is a link (cell at t) → (same cell at t+1). A predicted edge is a true positive only if both of its endpoints matched GT nodes and the corresponding GT nodes are actually connected by a GT edge.

edge_jaccard = TP / (TP + FP + FN)

This is the standard Jaccard (IoU) over the set of edges. It rewards the model for producing links that (a) connect real cells and (b) connect them the way the GT does. Getting a detection right but linking it to the wrong neighbour still costs you (FP + FN).

Your real edge numbers

"But if I detect everything, won't FP explode?" — the question you asked before. No, and here is the subtle part. The GT is sparse: only ~0.2% of the real cells are annotated. An edge is only counted as FP if its endpoints matched GT nodes but formed a wrong link. A predicted edge between two cells that the GT never annotated is not a per-edge FP — instead, over-detection is controlled by a separate, gentle node-count penalty (next section). That is exactly why the correct strategy is to over-detect toward the true cell count, not to detect only the ~600 annotated ones.

3. The node-count penalty → adjusted edge Jaccard

To stop you from spamming millions of detections, the edge Jaccard is scaled by how far your total node count is from the true cell count (estimated_number_of_nodes in the GEFF metadata — the real ~25k–65k, not the sparse annotation count):

node_ratio = (N_pred − N_estimated) / N_estimated
adj_edge_jaccard = max(0, edge_jaccard × (1 − 0.1 × node_ratio))
How to score well on this term: (1) get high node recall — every one of your predictions is ≥0.79, and three are ≥0.97, which is why edge recall is high; (2) keep N_pred ≈ N_estimated so node_ratio ≈ 0. 44b6_0113de3b nails this (ratio +0.003 → essentially zero penalty); 6bba_05b6850b over-detects 25% (ratio +0.25), shaving 0.95 → 0.93.

4. Stage 3 — Division Jaccard (the hard 10%)

A division (mitosis) is a cell that splits into two: in the graph, a node with out-degree 2. Divisions get their own Jaccard, worth 10% of the score:

division_jaccard = div_TP / (div_TP + div_FP + div_FN)

What counts as a division TP

Concretely (division_metrics.py): for each GT division the predicted graph is matched against that division's subgraph; it scores 1 only if a single connected predicted component covers (a) ≥1 node in the pre-split "one-node stage", and (b) ≥2 of the daughter lineages, and (c) contains an actual predicted fork (out-degree ≥ 2). A bipartite matching then ensures one predicted fork can't be credited to two GT divisions. div_FP = predicted forks whose matched GT cell isn't actually dividing.

Why divisions are so hard — three compounding reasons

  1. Extreme rarity (class imbalance). Divisions are 0.11% of nodes. A detector sees ~1000× more non-dividing cells, so there is almost no gradient signal to learn the "fork" pattern.
  2. It's an all-or-nothing structural event, not a point. To earn one TP you must simultaneously get the parent detection, the split moment, and both daughters linked correctly — miss any one and the whole event is an FN. A single wrong link anywhere in the parent→children→grandchildren structure loses the point.
  3. The Jaccard denominator is tiny, so misses are brutal. With only 3 events in these videos, recovering 0 gives 0/(0+0+3) = 0.00. There is no partial credit — you are at 0 until you nail an entire division end-to-end. (This is also why one lucky TP can swing the number a lot.)
How to actually get division points: because it's worth only 0.1× and is all-or-nothing, the highest-leverage path is (1) push node recall + linking quality near divisions so the daughter links exist at all, then (2) explicitly up-weight/oversample the rare division examples during training, and (3) at inference, allow out-degree-2 links (don't force one-to-one matching) so a genuine fork can be produced. Getting even a handful of the 3 events here from 0 → 1 would move division_jaccard 0.00 → 0.33 and the final score by +0.033.

6. TL;DR cheat-sheet

To maximise edge_jaccard: high node recall (detect all cells) + correct t→t+1 links.
To avoid the penalty: make N_pred ≈ estimated_number_of_nodes (over-detect toward the true ~25k–65k, not the sparse GT).
Coordinates: always score in microns at full resolution — undo any down-sampling first.
To score divisions: rare + structural + tiny denominator = hardest. Oversample divisions in training, keep daughter links, allow out-degree-2 at inference.
Weighting: edges dominate (×1), divisions are a ×0.1 bonus — but a fully-missed division term still caps you ~0.1 below the ceiling.
